commandWords.means: State the precise meaning of a geographical term.
commandWords.doThis: Give the exact technical definition in one sentence; do not use the word itself in the definition.

commandWords.means: Set out the characteristics of something using evidence, without explaining causes.
commandWords.doThis: State what a map, graph, photo or process shows, using figures, place names or directions; do not say why it happens.

commandWords.means: Give reasons for a pattern, process or feature, showing understanding of cause and effect.
commandWords.doThis: Use connectives such as 'this leads to' or 'because' to link a cause to its effect, ideally in a chain of at least two linked points.

commandWords.means: Consider the relative importance or success of factors and reach a supported judgement.
commandWords.doThis: Weigh up the different factors or impacts, use evidence for each, then conclude which matters most and why.

commandWords.means: Weigh up the extent to which a statement is true, considering different viewpoints.
commandWords.doThis: Give a balanced argument for and against, use named evidence for each side, then reach a justified overall conclusion that directly answers the question.

commandWords.means: Judge how far you agree with a statement, considering alternative views.
commandWords.doThis: Present the case that supports the statement, present the case against it, then give a final judgement stating a degree of agreement.

commandWords.means: Give reasons to support a choice or decision already made.
commandWords.doThis: State the decision, then give clear evidence-based reasons why it is the best option compared to alternatives.

commandWords.means: Break down information to show relationships between parts.
commandWords.doThis: Identify patterns, links or trends in the data and explain how different parts of the evidence relate to each other.

commandWords.means: Identify similarities and differences between two or more things.
commandWords.doThis: Use comparative language (e.g. 'whereas', 'similarly', 'in contrast') to directly link the two things, not two separate descriptions.

commandWords.means: Apply existing geographical knowledge to a new or unfamiliar situation.
commandWords.doThis: Use logical reasoning from concepts you know, even if the exact case has not been studied.

commandWords.means: You must refer specifically to the named resource, not just general knowledge.
commandWords.doThis: Quote data, labels or features directly from the figure, citing it by name, e.g. 'Figure 3 shows...'.

commandWords.word: Study Figure X and use your own knowledge
commandWords.means: Combine evidence from the given resource with case study knowledge you have learned.
commandWords.doThis: Start with a point from the figure, then add a supporting fact or figure from your own case study knowledge.

sections.title: Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
sections.note: Each entry is a real, locatable example with at least one figure or date, as required for Edexcel B extended answers.

items.detail: Hurricane Harvey hit Texas, USA in August 2017, causing over 100 fatalities and roughly $125 billion in damage from catastrophic flooding after over 1000mm of rainfall in parts of Houston.
Cyclone Idai struck Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Malawi in March 2019, killing over 1000 people and displacing around 400,000, destroying the port city of Beira.
The Kaikoura earthquake, New Zealand, magnitude 7.8, struck on 14 November 2016, killing 2 people and causing about NZ$2 billion of damage, with strong building codes limiting casualties.
The Haiti earthquake, magnitude 7.0, struck on 12 January 2010 near Port-au-Prince, killing an estimated 160,000-230,000 people due to poor building standards and weak emergency response.

India's GNI per capita was around US$2,390 (World Bank, Atlas method, recent data) with an HDI around 0.64 (medium-high), showing rapid IT and service-sector growth (e.g. Bangalore) alongside continued rural poverty.
Mumbai's population is around 20 million in its metropolitan area; Dharavi, one of its largest informal settlements, houses an estimated 700,000-1 million people in about 2.1 square kilometres.

Birmingham, UK's second largest city (population approximately 1.15 million), lost tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs from deindustrialisation from the 1970s-1990s, followed by regeneration schemes such as the Bullring (opened 2003) and HS2-linked investment.

items.term: Coastal management case study: Holderness coast
items.detail: The Holderness coast, East Yorkshire, erodes at an average rate of about 1.5-2 metres per year, among the fastest eroding coastlines in Europe; Mappleton has been protected since 1991 with rock groynes and a rock revetment.

The River Cherwell/Banbury flood scheme, or similarly the River Skerne, Darlington (naturalisation scheme, 1990s), used soft engineering to restore a meandering channel and floodplain storage to reduce downstream flood risk.
The Amazon rainforest lost roughly 11,000 square kilometres of forest cover in Brazil in a recent reported year (INPE data), driven mainly by cattle ranching and soy farming.
Alberta's Athabasca tar sands, Canada, produce over 3 million barrels of oil per day using energy-intensive extraction, generating higher carbon emissions per barrel than conventional oil.
The Sahara Desert biome (around 30 degrees N, area approximately 9.2 million square kilometres) sits under the descending, high-pressure limb of the Hadley cell, giving very low rainfall.
Usually 'define', 'identify' or 'give one reason' - state the fact directly with no development needed.
Usually 'describe' or 'explain'; give two developed points, each with a piece of evidence or a linked consequence (point-evidence or point-because).
Usually 'explain the impacts of...' - give three developed points, or two points each fully explained in a chain of cause and effect.
Extended writing, often 'assess' or 'explain', sometimes with a resource; needs a logical structure, developed points, and a brief conclusion.
One 8-mark question per paper also assesses spelling, punctuation and grammar (up to 4 extra marks) - use full sentences, paragraphs and geographical terminology accurately.
Requires a balanced discussion for and against, named located evidence on both sides, and a justified final judgement that directly answers the question.
Use the pre-released resource booklet; weigh named options against given criteria (e.g. cost, environmental impact, social impact) before justifying a final choice.

items.term: Marks for using case study place names
items.detail: Named, located, and dated detail (e.g. 'Cyclone Idai, Mozambique, March 2019') scores higher than generic, unnamed description.
A natural event that has the potential to threaten life or property.
The extent to which a community, area or system is susceptible to harm from a hazard.
The ability of a community or system to withstand, cope with and recover from a hazard event.
The increase in the proportion of a country's population living in urban areas.
A city with a population of more than 10 million people.
An area of housing built without legal permission, official planning or full access to services such as clean water and sanitation.
The difference in standards of living and wellbeing between the richest and poorest countries or regions in the world.
Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
The variety of plant and animal life in a particular habitat or ecosystem.
The rate at which plants store energy as biomass, after allowing for their own respiration, usually measured in grams per square metre per year.
Uninterrupted access to sufficient, affordable and reliable energy supplies to meet a country's needs.
The combination of different energy sources (e.g. coal, gas, renewables) that a country uses to meet its energy demand.
The zigzag transport of sediment along a coastline caused by waves approaching at an angle, moving material in the direction of the prevailing wind.
The volume of water flowing through a river cross-section per second, measured in cumecs (cubic metres per second).
The decline of manufacturing industry and its associated employment in a country or region.
A structured investigation of a geographical question using primary data collected in the field and secondary data, followed by analysis and evaluation.

sections.title: Fieldwork enquiry process: what each stage must contain

items.detail: State a clear, testable question or hypothesis linked to theory, e.g. 'quality of life decreases with distance from the CBD', and justify why the topic and location were chosen.
Give the physical/human background of the study area with a located map, explaining why it is suitable for testing the hypothesis.
State the sampling strategy used (random, systematic or stratified), justify why it suits the enquiry, and describe exactly how, where and how often data was collected.
Identify specific hazards (e.g. traffic, water, weather, lone working) and state the control measure taken to reduce each risk before fieldwork began.
Choose presentation techniques that suit the data type (e.g. choropleth for area data, scatter graph for correlation) and justify the choice.
Describe patterns and anomalies in the results using statistics (mean, median, range, Spearman's rank) and refer back to specific figures/graphs produced.
State clearly whether the original hypothesis is supported or rejected, using specific evidence from the analysis to justify the conclusion.
Assess the reliability and accuracy of the method, identify limitations (e.g. sample size, weather, human error, time of data collection), and suggest specific improvements.
For an urban quality of life enquiry: environmental quality surveys, questionnaires, and land use maps across the study transect from CBD to suburb.
For a river or coastal enquiry: measurements of channel width, depth, velocity, gradient or beach profile/sediment size at multiple sample sites along a transect.
Read the eastings (vertical gridline) value first, then the northings (horizontal gridline) value, giving the bottom-left corner of the grid square, e.g. 4523.
Estimate tenths across the square for eastings first, then tenths up the square for northings, giving a precise point, e.g. 452238.
1 cm on the map represents 50,000 cm (500 m) in real life; 2 cm represents 1 km.
1 cm on the map represents 25,000 cm (250 m) in real life; 4 cm represents 1 km.
Use a piece of string or ruler along the route (following curves for roads/rivers), measure its length, then convert using the map scale.
Lines join points of equal height; closely spaced contours show steep slopes, widely spaced contours show gentle slopes, and V-shapes pointing uphill often indicate a river valley.
Lay a strip of paper along the line, mark where each contour crosses it, transfer these marks to graph paper axes (distance vs height), then join with a smooth line.
Uses graded shading (usually darker = higher value) to show how a variable (e.g. population density) varies between defined areas such as wards or countries; needs a key with class intervals.
Uses circles or bars sized in proportion to a data value at a located point, useful for showing quantities like population or trade at specific places.
Comment on foreground, middle ground and background; identify physical and human features and their spatial relationship, avoiding vague terms like 'nice' or 'a lot'.
Bars usually show monthly precipitation (read against the left axis), the line shows monthly temperature (read against the right axis); state the range and pattern of both.
Identify peak rainfall, peak discharge, lag time (gap between the two peaks), rising limb and falling limb, and comment on how quickly discharge responds to rainfall.

sections.title: Statistics skills for fieldwork and data

items.detail: Add all the values together and divide by the number of values. Sensitive to extreme values (outliers).
Put the values in order; the middle value (or mean of the two middle values if an even number of data points). Not affected by outliers.
The value that occurs most often in the data set. Useful for categorical data.
Highest value minus lowest value; a simple measure of spread, but very sensitive to outliers.
Upper quartile minus lower quartile; measures the spread of the middle 50% of data and is less affected by outliers than the range.

Rank both data sets separately, find the difference in rank for each pair, square each difference, sum the squared differences, then apply the formula to give a value between -1 and +1 showing the strength and direction of correlation.

A result close to +1 shows strong positive correlation, close to -1 shows strong negative correlation, and close to 0 shows little or no correlation; always state what this means in the geographical context.
A data point that does not fit the general pattern; identify it, suggest a geographical or methodological reason for it, and consider whether to exclude it from analysis.

items.term: Why use inter-quartile range over range for fieldwork data
items.detail: IQR removes the influence of one or two extreme results (outliers) caused by measurement error or unusual local conditions, giving a fairer picture of typical spread.
State the factors or impacts you will weigh up in one introductory sentence, e.g. 'There are several reasons why..., including...'.

items.term: Structuring each point in an extended answer
items.detail: Point - explain why/how - support with named evidence or a figure - link back to the question (PEEL-style: point, evidence, explain, link).

items.term: Linking cause to effect in an explain answer
items.detail: Use 'this results in', 'this leads to', 'as a consequence' to build a chain rather than listing disconnected facts.
Briefly state both sides of the argument you will consider before beginning the detailed discussion.

items.term: Giving the case FOR in an evaluate answer
items.detail: Present the strongest arguments/evidence supporting the statement, each backed by a located example or figure.

items.term: Giving the case AGAINST in an evaluate answer
items.detail: Present counter-arguments or limitations with their own supporting evidence, showing genuine balance rather than a token sentence.

items.term: Concluding an evaluate/to what extent answer
items.detail: State a clear judgement (e.g. 'to a large extent', 'to a limited extent') and briefly justify why one side outweighs the other based on the evidence given.
Do not just describe both sides without judging between them; the mark scheme specifically rewards a justified final decision.

items.term: Using the resource booklet in Paper 3 decision-making
items.detail: Quote figures or named options directly from the booklet as evidence for your justification, rather than relying only on memorised case studies.

sections.title: Physical process sequences (cause and effect chains)

items.term: Formation of a headland and bay
items.detail: Alternating bands of hard and soft rock -> soft rock erodes faster by hydraulic action and abrasion -> bays form in the soft rock -> hard rock remains as headlands jutting into the sea.

Waves erode a notch at the base of a cliff by hydraulic action and abrasion -> the notch deepens undermining the rock above -> the unsupported cliff collapses -> repeated retreat leaves a gently sloping rock platform at the base.

A crack in a headland is widened by hydraulic action -> erosion enlarges the crack into a cave -> continued erosion breaks through the headland forming an arch -> wave action and weathering undermine the arch roof until it collapses leaving a stack -> further erosion of the stack's base leaves a stump.

Longshore drift transports sediment along the coast in the direction of the prevailing wind -> at a change in coastline direction (e.g. a river mouth) sediment continues to be deposited in open water -> a ridge builds up -> wind changes curve the end into a hook, forming a spit.

Slightly faster flow on the outside of a bend increases erosion (undercutting the bank) -> slower flow on the inside bend causes deposition -> the channel migrates sideways over time -> the bend becomes more pronounced.

Erosion narrows the neck of a meander -> during a flood the river cuts through the narrow neck taking the shortest path -> deposition seals off the old meander loop at both ends -> the old loop remains as a curved ox-bow lake.

Heavy or prolonged rainfall (or snowmelt) -> ground becomes saturated or is impermeable/urbanised so infiltration is reduced -> surface runoff increases rapidly -> river discharge rises faster than the channel can carry -> water overtops the banks causing flooding.

items.term: Subduction at a destructive plate boundary
items.detail: Denser oceanic crust meets less dense continental crust -> the oceanic plate is forced down (subducts) into the mantle -> friction and melting generate magma -> magma rises through the continental crust -> explosive volcanic eruptions and deep-focus earthquakes result.

Sea surface temperature exceeds about 27 degrees Celsius over deep warm water -> warm moist air rises rapidly creating an area of low pressure -> surrounding air rushes in and is deflected by the Coriolis effect, starting rotation -> rising air cools, condenses, releasing latent heat, which fuels further uplift -> the system intensifies into an organised tropical cyclone with an eye and eye wall.

High temperature and rainfall cause rapid decomposition of leaf litter -> nutrients are released quickly but taken up immediately by shallow tree roots -> most nutrients are stored in the biomass rather than the soil -> heavy rainfall leaches any remaining soil nutrients away -> soils become infertile if the forest is cleared.

1h 30m, worth 37.5% of the GCSE. Covers Hazardous Earth, Development Dynamics and Challenges of an Urbanising World. Roughly 1 minute per mark; allow extra time for the 8-mark and 12-mark extended answers, and check whether an 8-mark question carries SPaG marks.

1h 45m, worth 37.5% of the GCSE. Covers UK Physical Landscapes (coasts and rivers), the UK's Evolving Human Landscape, and the fieldwork-based Geographical Investigations section; budget extra time for the fieldwork questions referencing your own enquiries.

1h 30m, worth 25% of the GCSE. Covers People and Biomes, Forests Under Threat and Consuming Energy Resources, plus a pre-released resource booklet used for a decision-making exercise; read the whole booklet before answering the final extended question.

items.term: General timing rule for all three papers
items.detail: Roughly 1 minute per mark; spend the first few minutes reading the whole paper (and resource booklet for Paper 3) before writing, and leave time to check place names, dates and figures are accurate.
Underline the command word and mark allocation for every question first, so 'describe' answers are not accidentally explained and vice versa.

items.term: Equipment to bring for all three papers
items.detail: Pen, pencil, ruler, eraser and a sharpener; a calculator is allowed for statistics questions (e.g. Spearman's rank) on any paper.

items.term: Using case studies effectively under time pressure
items.detail: Keep a mental list of one named figure and one named date for each case study so located detail can be added quickly without lengthy recall.
The resource booklet for Paper 3 is issued shortly before the exam; read it thoroughly in the days before and annotate options against the likely decision-making criteria.

topics.name: Topic 1a Hazardous Earth: Climate and Tropical Cyclones
subtopics: Global atmospheric circulation: Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells
Low pressure at the equator, high pressure at 30 degrees, and the resulting climate zones
Ocean currents, the global conveyor belt and their role in redistributing heat
Natural climate change: orbital changes, volcanic activity, solar output, asteroid impacts
Evidence for climate change: ice cores, tree rings, historical records, sea level and glacial retreat
The enhanced greenhouse effect and human causes of climate change
Uneven global consequences of climate change for people and the environment
Distribution of tropical cyclones and the conditions needed to form them
Formation and structure of a tropical cyclone including the eye and eye wall
The Saffir-Simpson scale
Primary and secondary hazards: storm surge, high winds, intense rainfall, flooding, landslides
How physical and human factors affect vulnerability and resilience
Named case study of a tropical cyclone in a developed country
Named case study of a tropical cyclone in an emerging or developing country
Preparation, planning, prediction and protection responses

cards.front: Name the three cells of global atmospheric circulation.
cards.back: The Hadley cell, the Ferrel cell and the Polar cell.

cards.front: Why is there a belt of low pressure at the equator?
cards.back: Intense solar heating causes air to rise, creating low pressure, cloud and high rainfall.

cards.front: State four conditions needed for a tropical cyclone to form.
cards.back: Sea surface temperature above about 27 degrees Celsius, ocean depth of at least 60 to 70 metres, latitude between 5 and 30 degrees for the Coriolis effect, and low wind shear.

cards.front: What scale is used to classify tropical cyclones?
cards.back: The Saffir-Simpson scale, from category 1 to category 5, based on sustained wind speed.

cards.front: Describe conditions in the eye of a tropical cyclone.
cards.back: Calm, clear, descending air with the lowest pressure and no rain, surrounded by the most violent conditions in the eye wall.

cards.front: What is a storm surge and why is it so dangerous?
cards.back: A rise in sea level caused by low pressure and strong onshore winds; it causes rapid coastal flooding and is often the biggest cause of death.

cards.front: Give three types of evidence for past climate change.
cards.back: Ice cores, tree rings (dendrochronology), historical records, sea level change and glacial retreat.

cards.front: Name three natural causes of climate change.
cards.back: Orbital or Milankovitch cycles, volcanic eruptions releasing ash and aerosols, variations in solar output, and asteroid impacts.

cards.front: Why do developing countries often suffer greater cyclone impacts?
cards.back: Weaker building standards, poorer warning and evacuation systems, less money for defences, and greater dependence on agriculture for income.

cloze: The three cells of global atmospheric circulation are the {{c1::Hadley}}, {{c2::Ferrel}} and Polar cells.
Tropical cyclones need sea surface temperatures above about {{c1::27}} degrees Celsius.
Tropical cyclones are classified on the {{c1::Saffir-Simpson}} scale.
A {{c1::storm surge}} is a rise in sea level caused by low pressure and onshore winds.

topics.name: Topic 1b Hazardous Earth: Tectonic Hazards
subtopics: Internal structure of the Earth: inner core, outer core, mantle, crust
Convection currents, ridge push and slab pull as drivers of plate movement
Plate boundary types: divergent, convergent, conservative and collision
Distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes and their link to plate boundaries
Hotspots and intra-plate volcanic activity
Types of volcano and characteristic eruption styles
Primary and secondary earthquake hazards: ground shaking, liquefaction, tsunami, fires, disease
Measuring earthquakes and volcanic eruptions
Named case study of a tectonic hazard in a developed country
Named case study of a tectonic hazard in an emerging or developing country
Why people continue to live in tectonically active areas
Management: prediction, building design, planning, education and emergency response

cards.front: Name three mechanisms that move tectonic plates.
cards.back: Convection currents in the mantle, ridge push at constructive boundaries, and slab pull at destructive boundaries.

cards.front: What happens at a convergent oceanic-continental boundary?
cards.back: The denser oceanic plate subducts beneath the continental plate, causing deep earthquakes, explosive volcanoes and fold mountains.

cards.front: What happens at a divergent boundary?
cards.back: Plates move apart, magma rises to form new crust, producing shallow earthquakes and gentle volcanic activity, e.g. mid-ocean ridges.

cards.front: What is liquefaction?
cards.back: When violent ground shaking causes saturated loose soil to behave like a liquid, so buildings sink or tilt.

cards.front: Why do people continue to live in tectonically hazardous areas?
cards.back: Fertile volcanic soils, geothermal energy, tourism, mineral resources, family and cultural ties, and a belief that the risk is low or manageable.

cards.front: Give two ways buildings can be designed to resist earthquakes.
cards.back: Cross-bracing and shock absorbers or base isolators, deep foundations into bedrock, and lightweight roofing materials.

cards.front: Why is a collision boundary different from a convergent oceanic boundary?
cards.back: Two continental plates of similar density collide with no subduction, so crust buckles into fold mountains and there are earthquakes but no volcanoes.

cloze: At a {{c1::convergent}} boundary the denser oceanic plate {{c2::subducts}} beneath the continental plate.
{{c1::Slab pull}} and {{c2::ridge push}} act alongside mantle convection to move plates.
Violent shaking turning saturated soil into a fluid is called {{c1::liquefaction}}.

topics.name: Topic 2 Development Dynamics (India case study)
subtopics: Measuring development: GNI per capita, HDI, birth and death rates, literacy, life expectancy
Limitations of single indicators and the value of composite measures
The development gap and global patterns of inequality
Theories of development: Rostows modernisation model and Franks dependency theory
Demographic transition model stages and their link to development
Top-down versus bottom-up development strategies and their advantages
India: location, physical context, climate and population distribution
Indias changing economic sectors and the growth of manufacturing and services
The role of TNCs, globalisation and foreign direct investment in India
Advantages and disadvantages of TNC investment for India
Indias changing geopolitical role and regional relationships
Impacts of rapid growth on Indias environment and on inequality between states
Who benefits and who loses from rapid development

cards.front: What three measures combine to form the Human Development Index?
cards.back: Life expectancy at birth, education (mean and expected years of schooling), and GNI per capita.

cards.front: Why is GNI per capita alone a poor measure of development?
cards.back: It is a mean, so it hides inequality, ignores the informal economy, and says nothing about health, education or quality of life.

cards.front: Summarise Rostows modernisation model.
cards.back: Countries move through five stages - traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity, and age of mass consumption - as investment and industry grow.

cards.front: Summarise Franks dependency theory.
cards.back: Poorer countries remain poor because a core of wealthy nations extracts resources and value from a periphery, keeping it dependent.

cards.front: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of TNC investment in India.
cards.back: Advantages: employment and higher wages, transfer of skills and technology, multiplier effect. Disadvantages: profits leave the country, poor working conditions, environmental damage, and vulnerability if the TNC relocates.

cards.front: What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up development?
cards.back: Top-down is large scale, government or TNC-led and expensive, e.g. a dam; bottom-up is small scale, community-led and locally appropriate, e.g. a village water pump.

cards.front: What is the multiplier effect?
cards.back: Initial investment creates jobs and income, which is spent locally, creating further demand, jobs and tax revenue in a self-reinforcing cycle.

cloze: HDI combines life expectancy, {{c1::education}} and {{c2::GNI per capita}}.
{{c1::Rostow}} proposed a five-stage modernisation model of development.
{{c1::Bottom-up}} development is small scale and led by the local {{c2::community}}.
Initial investment generating further local income and jobs is the {{c1::multiplier}} effect.

topics.name: Topic 3 Challenges of an Urbanising World (Mumbai case study)
subtopics: Global urbanisation trends and contrasts between developed, emerging and developing countries
Causes of urbanisation: rural-urban migration and natural increase
Push and pull factors driving rural-urban migration
Megacities, world cities and their global distribution
Mumbai: site, situation, connectivity and reasons for growth
Mumbais land use pattern and functional zones
Quality of life contrasts within Mumbai
Dharavi as an informal settlement: housing, services, informal economy, recycling industry
Opportunities of living in Mumbai: employment, education, healthcare, services
Challenges: overcrowding, water and sanitation, traffic congestion, air pollution, informal work
Top-down redevelopment such as Vision Mumbai, and bottom-up self-help schemes
Making urban living more sustainable: transport, water, waste and energy

cards.front: Define urbanisation.
cards.back: The increase in the proportion of a countrys population living in urban areas.

cards.front: Define a megacity.
cards.back: A city with a population of more than 10 million people.

cards.front: Give three push and three pull factors for rural-urban migration.
cards.back: Push: lack of jobs, poor services, mechanisation of farming, drought or conflict. Pull: better paid work, education, healthcare, and perceived higher quality of life.

cards.front: Why did Mumbai grow so rapidly?
cards.back: A deep natural harbour and colonial port trade, then textile industry, Bollywood and financial services, plus continuing rural-urban migration and natural increase.

cards.front: Give two opportunities and two challenges of life in Dharavi.
cards.back: Opportunities: a large informal economy with recycling and small manufacturing, strong community networks. Challenges: extreme population density, inadequate sanitation and clean water, and insecure tenure.

cards.front: What was Vision Mumbai?
cards.back: A top-down redevelopment plan to improve Mumbai by replacing slums with high-rise housing and upgrading transport, sanitation and the economy.

cards.front: Why can top-down slum clearance be unpopular with residents?
cards.back: It can break up communities and informal businesses, replacement housing may be unaffordable or badly located, and residents are rarely consulted.

cloze: A {{c1::megacity}} has a population greater than {{c2::10 million}}.
Mumbai grew initially because of its deep natural {{c1::harbour}} and colonial trade.
{{c1::Dharavi}} is a large informal settlement in Mumbai known for its {{c2::recycling}} industry.
{{c1::Urbanisation}} is an increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas.

topics.name: Topic 6 Geographical Investigations (Human and Physical Fieldwork)
subtopics: Formulating a geographical question or hypothesis
Sampling strategies: random, systematic, stratified, and justifying the choice
Quantitative methods: counts, measurements, questionnaires with closed questions
Qualitative methods: field sketches, photographs, environmental quality surveys, interviews
Risk assessment and how risks are reduced
Human fieldwork enquiry: variations in quality of life within an urban area
Physical fieldwork enquiry: coastal or river landscape processes and management
Secondary data sources: census data, Environment Agency data, OS maps, GIS
Presenting data: located bars, choropleth, proportional symbols, scatter graphs, radar charts
Analysis using measures of central tendency, range and interquartile range
Drawing conclusions that answer the original question
Evaluating reliability, accuracy, limitations and how the enquiry could be improved
Map skills: four and six figure grid references, scale, distance, direction, relief and contours

cards.front: Define stratified sampling in fieldwork.
cards.back: Dividing the study area or population into subgroups and sampling each in proportion to its size, so all groups are represented.

cards.front: Why is systematic sampling used along a river or transect?
cards.back: It gives evenly spaced measurements, which makes it easy to show change with distance and to replicate.

cards.front: Give two limitations of using questionnaires in an urban quality of life enquiry.
cards.back: Responses are subjective and may be biased, and the sample may not be representative if it is collected at one time of day or place.

cards.front: What is a choropleth map best used for?
cards.back: Showing how a quantity varies between defined areas using graded shading, e.g. population density by ward.

cards.front: Why must a risk assessment be completed before fieldwork?
cards.back: To identify hazards such as traffic, deep or fast-flowing water, and weather, and to plan measures that reduce the likelihood or severity of harm.

cards.front: What is the difference between reliability and accuracy in fieldwork data?
cards.back: Reliability is whether repeating the method gives consistent results; accuracy is how close the measurement is to the true value.

cards.front: How do you give a six-figure grid reference?
cards.back: Eastings first then northings; read the two-digit gridline then estimate tenths across the square, for both axes.

cloze: {{c1::Systematic}} sampling takes measurements at regular intervals, for example every 100 metres.
A {{c1::choropleth}} map uses graded shading to show how a value varies between areas.
Grid references are read {{c1::eastings}} before {{c2::northings}}.
Data collected by someone else, such as census figures, is {{c1::secondary}} data.

topics.name: Paper 3 People and Environment Issues (Topics 7, 8 and 9)
subtopics: Topic 7: global distribution of major biomes and the factors that control it
Net primary productivity and how it varies between biomes
How humans use and modify biomes, including biotic resources and food, energy and water demand
Topic 8: structure and layers of the tropical rainforest and its nutrient cycle
Rainforest adaptations of plants and animals and high biodiversity

cards.front: What two climatic factors most strongly control global biome distribution?
cards.back: Temperature and precipitation, which are largely determined by latitude and global atmospheric circulation.

cards.front: Why are rainforest soils infertile despite dense vegetation?
cards.back: Nutrients are stored in the biomass, not the soil; rapid decomposition and heavy leaching mean nutrients are taken up immediately or washed away.

cards.front: Give four causes of tropical deforestation.
cards.back: Commercial logging, cattle ranching and soy or palm oil plantations, mineral extraction, hydroelectric and road development, and subsistence farming or settlement.

cards.front: Why does the taiga have low biodiversity?
cards.back: Long cold winters, a short growing season, acidic nutrient-poor podsol soils and limited water availability when frozen restrict the range of species.

cards.front: What is selective logging and why is it more sustainable?
cards.back: Only mature or lower-value trees are felled, leaving the canopy and younger trees intact so the forest regenerates and habitat is retained.

cards.front: Define energy security.
cards.back: Uninterrupted access to sufficient, affordable and reliable energy supplies to meet a countrys needs.

cards.front: Give two environmental costs of extracting oil from tar sands.
cards.back: Large-scale removal of boreal forest and soil, high water use and toxic tailings ponds, and high carbon emissions per barrel produced.

cards.front: What does the Paper 3 12-mark decision-making question require?
cards.back: Use the resource booklet to weigh the given options against stated criteria such as cost, environment and people, choose one, justify it with evidence, and acknowledge its drawbacks and the rejected options.

cards.front: What is net primary productivity?
cards.back: The rate at which plants store energy as biomass after their own respiration, usually measured in grams per square metre per year.

cloze: Rainforest nutrients are stored mainly in the {{c1::biomass}} rather than the {{c2::soil}}.
The taiga has {{c1::low}} biodiversity because of its short growing season and acidic {{c2::podsol}} soils.

cards.front: Name the four coastal erosion processes.
cards.back: Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution.

cards.front: Describe the sequence forming a stack.
cards.back: A crack in a headland is widened by erosion into a cave, the cave erodes through to form an arch, the arch roof collapses leaving a stack, which is undercut to leave a stump.

cards.front: What is longshore drift?
cards.back: The zigzag movement of sediment along a coast caused by waves approaching at an angle, with swash moving material diagonally up the beach and backwash returning it straight down.

cards.front: Compare hard and soft engineering.
cards.back: Hard engineering uses built structures such as sea walls and groynes - effective but expensive and often visually intrusive. Soft engineering works with natural processes, e.g. beach nourishment or managed retreat - cheaper and more sustainable but less immediately protective.

cards.front: How does an ox-bow lake form?
cards.back: Erosion on the outside bends narrows the meander neck until a flood cuts through; deposition then seals off the old meander, leaving a curved lake.

cards.front: What does lag time on a hydrograph mean, and what shortens it?
cards.back: The time between peak rainfall and peak discharge. Impermeable rock, steep slopes, urbanisation, saturated or frozen ground and deforestation all shorten it, increasing flood risk.

cards.front: What is deindustrialisation and how did it affect Birmingham?
cards.back: The decline of manufacturing employment. In Birmingham it caused job losses in car and metal industries, unemployment and derelict land, later addressed by service-sector growth and city-centre regeneration.

cards.front: What is rural rebranding?
cards.back: Changing the image and function of a rural area, often through tourism, heritage or specialist food production, to attract visitors and investment.
